summary: Defines terms for benchmarking how quickly link-state routing protocols like IS-IS and OSPF settle on new routes after a change. The measurements are black-box and look only at data-plane behavior seen from outside. It is the vocabulary document for the methods in RFC 6413.

plainLanguage.summary: When a road closes, drivers need to find a new route, and how fast they all agree varies. This sets out the words used to measure how fast routers agree on new paths, so testers speak the same language.

questions: how to measure route convergence time
what is the difference between rate-derived and loss-derived methods
subtitle: The shared vocabulary for timing how fast routers settle on new paths, measured only from outside the router.

tldr.problem: Measuring how quickly a link-state routing protocol such as IS-IS or OSPF recovers from a change is only comparable between routers if testers use the same words and the same instants.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines terms for convergence types, key instants, interfaces, three measurement methods and the resulting time benchmarks, all derived from data-plane traffic seen at a Tester.
tldr.outcome: It is the terminology companion to RFC 6413, which supplies the test methodology.

facts.label: Validation time
facts.value: 5 consecutive packets per destination, minimum 5 seconds

today: RFC 6412 is an Informational document and the metadata shows no obsoleting or updating RFC. Use it alongside RFC 6413, which gives the test procedures.

sections.title: Scope and Purpose
sections.content:
RFC 6412 is the companion to RFC 6413. It introduces the terms needed to run that methodology for benchmarking link-state Interior Gateway Protocol (IGP) route convergence. Convergence time is measured by watching the data plane through the Device Under Test (DUT) at a Tester, so the router's internals are never inspected (black-box testing).

The terms apply to IPv4 and IPv6 traffic and to link-state IGPs such as IS-IS and OSPF. The document reuses existing benchmarking terms such as Throughput, Offered Load, Forwarding Rate and Forwarding Delay from earlier RFCs. It uses RFC 2119 keywords although it is not a Standards Track document.
sections.plainLanguage: The testers watch cars leaving a junction from the outside. They never look inside the traffic controller, so any router brand can be compared fairly.

sections.title: Convergence, Instants and Interfaces
sections.content:
Route Convergence is the process of updating all router components, including the RIB and FIB and software and hardware tables, so that forwarding for a route succeeds on the Next-Best Egress Interface. Full Convergence is Route Convergence for all routes in the FIB. The test cases are built so that convergence changes the egress interface, which makes it visible from outside.

The RFC defines moments in time. The Traffic Start Instant is when the Tester sends the first data packet. The Convergence Event Instant is when the event occurs. The First Route Convergence Instant is when the first route completes convergence. The Convergence Recovery Instant is when Full Convergence has completed, and it must hold for the Sustained Convergence Validation Time. Two transitions describe the Forwarding Rate falling on the Preferred Egress Interface and rising again.

The Preferred Egress Interface carries the traffic before the event. The Next-Best Egress Interface is the interface, or the set of interfaces in an ECMP or parallel link set, for the second-best next hop. A Local Interface is on the DUT, while a Remote Interface is on a neighbor that is not directly connected to it.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine timing a detour. You note when the road closed, when the first car found the new way, and when all cars were using it steadily. Each of those moments has its own name.

sections.title: Three Measurement Methods
sections.content:
The Rate-Derived Method computes benchmarks by observing the Forwarding Rate in every Packet Sampling Interval. At least one packet per route must be offered within each interval, and the interval should be as small as possible, though IP Packet Delay Variation (IPDV) may force a larger one. It should not be used for route-specific measurements.

The Loss-Derived Method computes benchmarks from the number of Impaired Packets. It only gives averages over all routes, and it should be combined with the Rate-Derived Method to see when Full Convergence completes.

The Route-Specific Loss-Derived Method gives each stream a single destination matching one route and measures loss per stream. It is the RECOMMENDED method for convergence time benchmarks because it observes loss as a network user would experience it.
sections.plainLanguage: One way is to count cars passing each minute. Another is to count the cars that got lost along the way. The best way is to follow one car for each destination and see how long that car waited.

sections.title: Benchmarks and Measurement Terms
sections.content:
Full Convergence Time is the Convergence Recovery Instant minus the Convergence Event Instant, and First Route Convergence Time is the First Route Convergence Instant minus the Convergence Event Instant. Both come from the Rate-Derived Method. Route-Specific Convergence Time is computed per route from Connectivity Packet Loss divided by the Offered Load per route, and Loss-Derived Convergence Time is the same idea averaged over all routes. If the event does not cause instant loss, the gap between Traffic Start Instant and Convergence Event Instant is subtracted.

The Route Loss of Connectivity Period is how long packets to one route were impaired. It can be shorter than the convergence time if traffic keeps flowing on the Preferred Egress Interface for a while.

An Impaired Packet is lost, too late, corrupted, duplicated or out of order. The Forwarding Delay Threshold decides when a late packet counts as lost and MUST be reported. The recommended Sustained Convergence Validation Time is the time to send 5 consecutive packets to each destination, with a minimum of 5 seconds, based on RFC 2544, which suggests waiting 2 seconds for residual frames and 5 seconds for DUT restabilization.
sections.plainLanguage: The score is simple subtraction: the time the new route works minus the time the old one broke. Packets that arrive broken, late or in the wrong order count as 'lost' for the score.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Benchmarking is limited to controlled laboratory tests with dedicated address space. The test network MUST NOT be connected to devices that could forward test traffic into a production network or misroute it to the test management network. Tests are black-box, and the DUT SHOULD NOT have special capabilities for benchmarking, so its security implications are the same in the lab and in production.
sections.plainLanguage: Run the experiment in a closed test room so none of the practice traffic leaks out to the real roads.

items.title: Rate-Derived
items.text: Watches Forwarding Rate each Packet Sampling Interval. Gives First Route and Full Convergence Time.

items.title: Loss-Derived
items.text: Counts Impaired Packets. Gives an average over all routes.

items.title: Route-Specific Loss-Derived
items.text: One stream per route. Recommended for convergence time and loss of connectivity.
